steps.title: Пассив во временах
steps.html:
ВремяФормаПример
Present simpleam / is / are + past participleThe hat is pulled over the head.
Past simplewas / were + past participleFive thousand pillows were shipped.
Present perfecthas / have been + past participle$195,000 has been pledged.
Present continuousis / are being + past participleMore are being manufactured.
Будущее и модальныеwill be / can be / must be + past participleIt can be seen from the road.

steps.title: Как это работает
steps.html:
Пассив нужен, когда исполнитель неизвестен, очевиден или не важен. The building was renovated in 2019 — строители здесь не главное.

by добавляется, только если исполнителя стоит назвать: pledged by its backers. В большинстве пассивных предложений by нет вовсе.

Чтобы построить пассив, дополнение активного предложения становится подлежащим: Strangers funded the project → The project was funded.

Глаголы без дополнения не имеют пассива: happen, arrive, seem, rise, go.

steps.title: The crowd will pay for it
steps.html:
A hat that lets you sleep at your desk raised nearly two hundred thousand dollars from strangers. Most projects are not so lucky.

A  The Ostrich Pillow was invented to solve a problem that no bank would have taken seriously. Its designer had noticed that people who travel a lot get very tired, and that there is nowhere to put your head. The result is a padded hat that is pulled over the head so that the wearer can take a nap almost anywhere. It looks ridiculous, which is part of the point. More than nineteen hundred people paid for one before a single unit had been manufactured.

B  This is how crowd-funding works. An idea is presented directly to the people who might buy it, usually as a short film and a page of drawings. Money is pledged rather than paid: nothing is taken from anyone unless the target is reached by the deadline. If it is, the money is released and production begins. If it is not, every pledge is returned and the project quietly disappears. Nothing is guaranteed to anybody at any stage.

C  For a designer who is short of cash, the attraction is obvious. A bank loan must be applied for, defended and repaid whatever happens; a crowd-funded product is paid for by the people who actually want it. But the real value is often information rather than money. If two thousand strangers will pay in advance for something that does not yet exist, the idea has been tested before a factory is booked. If only forty will, that is worth knowing too, and it has cost almost nothing to find out.

D  The failure rate is high and is not usually mentioned in the success stories. Only around a third of projects reach their target, and reaching it is not the end of the difficulty. Products that were designed in a bedroom have to be manufactured, packed and shipped to thousands of addresses in dozens of countries, often by people who have never done any of that before. Deliveries are regularly delayed by a year or more, and backers are told about the problem long after they were told about the triumph.

E  Platforms have been criticised for this. Their defenders answer that a pledge is not a purchase: backers are supporting an attempt, not ordering from a shop, and that distinction is printed clearly on every page. Critics reply that it is not how the pages are read, and that a page filled with photographs of a finished-looking product is understood as an advertisement whatever the small print says.

F  What has genuinely changed is who gets to try. Fifty years ago an unusual idea had to be presented to somebody with money, and most such ideas were refused by people who were paid to be careful. Now they are refused, or backed, by the public. The Ostrich Pillow was rejected by every manufacturer its designer approached. Then it was funded in three weeks by strangers, and has since been sold in more than fifty countries.

Deliveries are regularly delayed by a year or more, and backers are told about the problem long after they were told about the triumph.

E  Platforms have been criticised for this. Their defenders answer that a pledge is not a purchase: backers are supporting an attempt, not ordering from a shop, and that distinction is printed clearly on every page. Critics reply that it is not how the pages are read, and that a page filled with photographs of a finished-looking product is understood as an advertisement whatever the small print says.

F  What has genuinely changed is who gets to try. Fifty years ago an unusual idea had to be presented to somebody with money, and most such ideas were refused by people who were paid to be careful. Now they are refused, or backed, by the public. The Ostrich Pillow was rejected by every manufacturer its designer approached. Then it was funded in three weeks by strangers, and has since been sold in more than fifty countries.
